title: Food Prices Rise Again as Fuel Costs More

source.author: Sam Silverstein
source.title: Consumers face higher grocery prices
source.checked_against: Single source: a news report of the October Consumer Price Index data. Figures come only from this article; the government tables were not opened. Bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, ham, poultry and the fuel price per gallon are left out. 'Lettuce' is written as 'salad leaves' and 'diesel' as 'one kind of fuel' to stay inside the reader's vocabulary.

paragraphs: Food prices in American supermarkets rose again this autumn. Food that people buy to eat at home cost 0.4 percent more in October than in September. That may sound small, but it is not a mere detail. It was the largest monthly increase since April. The figures come from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, and Retail Dive reported them.
Usually, the office also compares prices with the same month one year earlier. This time it could not. In October 2025 the government was closed for a time, so nobody collected price data that month.

Vegetables illustrate the problem well. Prices for fresh vegetables rose more than 2 percent in one month. Salad leaves were a remarkable case: they cost almost 8 percent more. Fresh fruit showed a distinct trend. Contrary to vegetable prices, fruit prices went down in October. Apple prices, for example, slipped 1.6 percent.

Meat prices have risen repeatedly this year, and October was no different. Ground beef cost about 1 percent more. Beef steak rose almost 2 percent. Coffee did not follow the trend. On the contrary, coffee prices decreased about 3.5 percent.

Why is food more expensive? The report traces the increase to fuel. One kind of fuel is not a mere extra cost for food companies. They need it to produce food and to deliver it to stores. In early November, this fuel cost 60 percent more than a year earlier.

The year has been a mixture of rises and falls. Food prices went up in January and February. In April they jumped almost 1 percent, when the war in Iran hurt oil supplies. The increase was slower in May and June. Then prices slipped slightly in July and again in September. In other words, prices have changed direction repeatedly in 2026.

FMI is a trade group for the food industry. It says that food stores are working hard to keep prices under control. They also want to keep supplies steady, even when fuel costs more. In September, the group said that food prices would rise faster later in 2026. The reason was simple. Stores and suppliers had paid higher costs for months, and they would begin to pass them on to shoppers.

Andy Harig of FMI highlights the delay. When fuel prices rise, it costs more to grow food and to transport it. Nevertheless, shoppers do not see the change at once. It can take months before higher costs appear in store prices. The October figures illustrate this delay, and many experts trace it back to fuel. A mixture of cheaper fruit and more expensive vegetables and meat is what shoppers found this autumn. A bag of salad leaves now shows how far the price of fuel can travel.
